questions.q: How did the decline of the Mughal Empire reshape India's political map?
answer: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, the Mughal Empire weakened rapidly, and its place was taken by many regional powers.

answer.text: Weak successors and court rivalries were worsened by invasions — Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739, carrying off the Peacock Throne and the Kohinoor, and Ahmad Shah Abdali repeatedly attacked, defeating the Marathas at Panipat in 1761.
Successor states such as Hyderabad, Awadh and Bengal broke away, while new powers like the Marathas, Sikhs and Jats rose in opposition. No single authority remained.
This fragmentation allowed the English East India Company, after Plassey and Buxar and the grant of the Diwani in 1765, to begin its rise to power.

questions.q: How did new regional states emerge from the decline of the Mughal Empire, and what kinds were they?

answer.text: after Aurangzeb, powerful governors and local chiefs carved out states that were nominally under the emperor but effectively independent. Historians group them into broad types.

list: Old Mughal provinces where governors became near-independent, such as Hyderabad under Nizam-ul-Mulk, Awadh under Sa'adat Khan and Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan
Watan jagirs of established Rajput houses like Amber and Jodhpur that asserted greater autonomy
New states set up by rebellion against the Mughals, such as those of the Marathas, Sikhs and Jats

answer.text: these states shared features — they raised revenue efficiently, built armies and courts — but their rivalries and the Mughal collapse left India divided and open to Company expansion.

questions.q: What common features of governance did the eighteenth-century successor states share?

answer.lead: The new states borrowed from Mughal practice
answer.text: even as they broke from it. Their rulers needed money and soldiers, so they reformed administration to secure both.

list: Many used revenue farmers or 'ijaradars' to collect taxes, though this could burden peasants
They entered into close ties with rich bankers and merchants who lent money and managed revenues
They built up their own armies and appointed loyal officials, reducing dependence on the Mughal centre

answer.text: made the states militarily strong but also dependent on financiers, and their mutual rivalries prevented any single power from replacing the Mughals — an opening the Company exploited.
